displayQuote: He who has a why to live can bear almost any how

meta.title: Who really said "He who has a why to live can bear almost any how"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Nietzsche — Twilight of the Idols (1889), Maxims and Arrows 12. But the famous English wording isn't from any Nietzsche translation: it descends from Ilse Lasch's 1959 translation of Viktor Frankl's Man's Search for Meaning, and is in copyright.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'He who has a why to live can bear almost any how'?
meta.ogDescription: Nietzsche wrote it (Twilight of the Idols, 1889) — but the English everyone quotes comes from Frankl's translator, not Nietzsche's, and it's still in copyright. Public-domain renderings read very differently.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The aphorism is genuinely his — Götzen-Dämmerung (Twilight of the Idols), written 1888 and published January 1889, ‘Sprüche und Pfeile’ (Maxims and Arrows) No. 12: “Hat man sein warum? des Lebens, so verträgt man sich fast mit jedem wie?” The twist is the English: the wording everyone quotes is not from any translation of Nietzsche. It descends from Ilse Lasch’s 1959 translation of Viktor Frankl’s Man’s Search for Meaning, where Frankl quotes him.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Götzen-Dämmerung (Twilight of the Idols), ‘Sprüche und Pfeile’ No. 12
Ilse Lasch, 1959 — translating Viktor Frankl, not Nietzsche

source.excerpt: Hat man sein warum? des Lebens, so verträgt man sich fast mit jedem wie? — Der Mensch strebt nicht nach Glück; nur der Engländer tut das.
trail: The German is Maxims and Arrows No. 12 of Götzen-Dämmerung — and note the second half, almost never quoted: ‘Man does not strive for happiness; only the Englishman does that.’ The aphorism is a joke at England’s expense as much as a maxim about endurance German text ↗.

No Nietzsche translator produced the famous sentence. Ludovici (1911, public domain) has ‘If a man knows the wherefore of his existence, then the manner of it can take care of itself’; Kaufmann (1954) ‘If we have our own why of life…’; Hollingdale (1968) ‘If we possess our why of life…’ Ludovici 1911 ↗.

The wording in circulation traces instead to Ilse Lasch’s 1959 English of Frankl’s Man’s Search for Meaning: ‘He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how.’ The popular form drops Lasch’s ‘for’ and ‘with.’ The Nietzsche quote the anglophone world knows is really Frankl’s translator’s sentence Quote Investigator ↗.
source.excerptNote: Maxims and Arrows No. 12 entire, in Nietzsche’s German. The famous half is the first clause; the second is a jab at English utilitarianism that quotation almost always discards.
source.rightsHolder: Ilse Lasch translation (Beacon Press) — for the popular English wording
source.rightsNote: Split, and this is the part people get wrong. Nietzsche’s German is public domain worldwide — he died in 1900 — so you may quote and translate the original freely. But the English sentence you are almost certainly about to use is not his translator’s and is still in copyright: it descends from Ilse Lasch’s 1959 rendering of Frankl. Kaufmann (1954) and Hollingdale (1968) are also protected. For a genuinely free English text use Ludovici’s 1911 translation — ‘If a man knows the wherefore of his existence, then the manner of it can take care of itself’ — or translate the German yourself. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
author.heading: About Friedrich Nietzsche
author.bio: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) wrote Twilight of the Idols in a few weeks in 1888, months before the collapse that ended his working life. Its opening section, ‘Maxims and Arrows,’ is a run of single-sentence provocations, of which this is the twelfth. Its modern fame is largely secondhand: Viktor Frankl quoted it in Man’s Search for Meaning, and it is Frankl’s translator’s English, not Nietzsche’s translators’, that the world memorised.

misattribution.heading: Right philosopher, borrowed English
misattribution.intro: The attribution is correct: Nietzsche wrote this. What almost nobody realises is that the English sentence they are quoting was written seventy years later, by a translator working on a different book.

items.why: ‘He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how’ is Lasch’s English in Man’s Search for Meaning, where Frankl quotes Nietzsche. No Nietzsche translation reads this way, and the popular form trims her ‘for’ and ‘with’ translation history ↗.

The aphorism continues: ‘Man does not strive for happiness; only the Englishman does that.’ The quotation always stops before the joke, which changes a barbed aside into a piece of pure uplift German original ↗.

True of the German, false of the sentence being reproduced. The popular English descends from a 1959 translation still in copyright; the free alternative, Ludovici’s 1911, reads quite differently public-domain text ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols (1889), Maxims and Arrows 12 — but the famous English is Frankl’s translator’s, and is in copyright. Use the German, or Ludovici’s 1911 rendering, to reuse it freely translation history ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Frankl is the reason it matters to most people. He used it in Man’s Search for Meaning to describe what distinguished those who survived the camps — not strength or optimism, but having something specific left to live for. In that setting the line stops being an aphorism and becomes a clinical observation.

Nietzsche’s own use was lighter and more sardonic, sitting in a run of one-line provocations and turning immediately into a joke about the English. The sentence acquired its gravity from the man who borrowed it.
context.detailsSummary: Five English versions of the same sentence
detailsBody: German (1889): ‘Hat man sein warum? des Lebens, so verträgt man sich fast mit jedem wie?’
Thomas Common (1896): ‘When one has one’s wherefore of life, one gets along with almost every how.’
Ludovici (1911, public domain): ‘If a man knows the wherefore of his existence, then the manner of it can take care of itself.’
Kaufmann (1954): ‘If we have our own why of life, we shall get along with almost any how.’
Ilse Lasch, translating Frankl (1959): ‘He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how’ — the ancestor of the popular form.
context.pull: The Nietzsche quote everyone knows is really Frankl's translator's sentence.
